title: CAP and consistency
objective: See the choice a network partition forces: keep answering and let copies drift, or stay consistent and refuse requests.

sources.title: Gilbert and Lynch (2002), Brewer's conjecture and the feasibility of consistent, available, partition-tolerant web services, ACM SIGACT News
Brewer (2012), CAP Twelve Years Later: How the "Rules" Have Changed (InfoQ / IEEE Computer)

simplifies: Two copies, one on each side, and every write must be confirmed by both to count as consistent. Real systems use majorities (quorums), so the larger side can keep working; they reconcile after healing with timestamps, version vectors or merge rules. As Brewer notes, partitions are rare, so the choice only bites while one is happening.

challenges.title: Stay available
challenges.prompt: The network between the sides will be cut 3 seconds in. Keep refused requests at 1% or less the whole time for 8 seconds after that.

predict.prompt: Consistent mode is on, and the two copies can't reach each other. What happens to writes?

options.text: They are refused, because they can't be confirmed by the other side
options.explanation: Right. Consistency means refusing rather than risking two different answers.
There is no link to sync over.

options.text: They go to the other side

challenges.hint: What if each side just answered on its own?
challenges.explain: In available mode each side keeps accepting writes, so nobody is refused. Now look at "Writes only one side has": the copies are drifting apart, and someone will have to reconcile them later.

challenges.title: Stay consistent
challenges.prompt: Same cut. Now keep the two copies identical (no writes on only one side) the whole time for 8 seconds after the cut.

predict.prompt: In available mode, both sides keep accepting writes during the cut. What happens to the two copies?

options.text: They drift apart: each has writes the other doesn't
options.explanation: Right. With no link, neither side sees the other's writes.
Only if they could talk to each other.
Nothing deletes them; they simply differ.

challenges.hint: You can keep the copies identical only by not accepting writes you can't share.
challenges.explain: Consistent mode keeps the copies identical, but it refuses writes during the cut: the refused requests are the price. Together, the two challenges show that during a partition you can't have both.

quiz.prompt: During a network partition, a system must choose between…

options.text: Answering every request (availability) and every answer agreeing (consistency)
options.explanation: Right. With the copies cut off from each other, it can't guarantee both.
That is a real trade-off, but not the CAP one.
Both kinds face the same choice during a partition.

quiz.prompt: A bank account balance during a partition: which choice usually makes sense?

options.text: Refuse risky writes (stay consistent), so money can't be spent twice
options.explanation: Right. For balances, a wrong answer costs more than a refused request.

options.text: Accept every write and fix it later
options.explanation: Two sides could both approve spending the same money.
Only the writes that can't be confirmed need refusing.
